clips.stepText: After eating, you can run after a football. Your cells unlock some energy stored in food so your muscles can work.

clips.stepText: Getting air into your chest helps because your tissues need oxygen. The work still happens inside your cells. When you kick a football, your muscle needs an energy carrier it can use immediately. We call that carrier ATP.

clips.stepText: Oxygen matters because it lets the cell finish gathering much more usable energy from its fuel. Think of a leg muscle during a steady walk. The first stage starts in the fluid inside the cell. Much of the later work depends on mitochondria.

clips.stepText: Yeast still needs a small supply of usable energy when oxygen is unavailable. Think about bubbles that make bread dough rise. The escaping gas is carbon dioxide. Ethanol is another product, even though you mainly notice the bubbles.

clips.stepText: A fast sprint can demand energy sooner than the aerobic pathway can supply it. Think of chasing a loose ball. Your muscles can keep the first stage going by forming lactate. That is a different outcome from the one you see in bread dough.

clips.stepText: Why does the cell need another stage after splitting glucose? Much of the fuel’s energy is still available. Think of a muscle cell on a steady walk. It passes some of that energy to small carriers for use in the next stage.

clips.stepText: Why does the dough get bigger? Follow what fills the holes. Yeast can make a gas as it uses sugar. The gas collects inside the dough, so you can use the rising as a clue even without seeing the individual cells.

clips.stepText: The organism and the oxygen clue work together. First settle which pathway fits yeast here. The gas is already named, so set it aside. Think of the other compound formed in that pathway. You need the one associated with yeast rather than muscle cells.

clips.stepText: The question asks what the cell can use to pay for work. Look carefully at the endings of those nearly identical names. Extra phosphate changes what the molecule can do. Heat can accompany the process, but it is a different kind of answer.

clips.stepText: The absence of oxygen is only one clue. Look at the living thing as well. If the question moves from dough to a working muscle, do not carry over the same second product. The pathways end in different compounds.

clips.stepText: Start by asking whether the pathway can use oxygen. Then check which living thing is doing the work. Remember the dough and the sprint. They give you two different clues for the products when the question describes energy release without relying on oxygen.

clips.stepText: Touch a hot pot and your hand pulls away quickly. Your body gets messages to the right parts so they can work together.

clips.stepText: A message needs a route so the correct part can respond. Think of turning your head towards a sudden clap. Signals can run along nerve cells. Where one ends, a chemical can cross the small gap to pass the news on.

clips.stepText: A quick escape matters when something could hurt you. Think of your finger meeting a hot pot. A short route through the spinal cord lets the muscle get moving while information is still travelling towards the brain.
clips.mathToSpeechText: A quick escape matters when something could hurt you. Think of your finger meeting a hot pot. A short route through the spinal cord lets the muscle get moving while information is still travelling towards the brain.
clips.spokenLine: A quick escape matters when something could hurt you. Think of your finger meeting a hot pot. A short route through the spinal cord lets the muscle get moving while information is still travelling towards the brain.

clips.stepText: Blood reaches many places, so a signal needs a way to select its audience. After a meal, for example, insulin can reach many tissues. Cells respond if they can recognise that message. The recognising structures are called receptors.

clips.stepText: Your muscles need good timing even when you already know what to do. Think of catching a ball as you step sideways. Your balance and hand movement have to fit together. The cerebellum helps make that adjustment.
clips.mathToSpeechText: Your muscles need good timing even when you already know what to do. Think of catching a ball as you step sideways. Your balance and hand movement have to fit together. The cerebellum helps make that adjustment.

clips.stepText: The body needs to deal with glucose entering the blood after food. Think of eating a bowl of rice. Some tissues take up more glucose when they receive the insulin signal. The body can keep some as a stored carbohydrate called glycogen.
clips.mathToSpeechText: The body needs to deal with glucose entering the blood after food. Think of eating a bowl of rice. Some tissues take up more glucose when they receive the insulin signal. The body can keep some as a stored carbohydrate called glycogen.

clips.stepText: Why pull back before thinking it through? A delay would keep your skin on the heat. Begin where you felt the danger, then trace the message inwards. Now follow the return journey to the muscle. The short circuit gives you a fast response.

clips.stepText: Start with the job you could watch. Is the body keeping its balance and making a controlled movement? That is the clue for this brain region. A reflex has a different route. Hormone control points you towards other parts of the brain.

clips.stepText: Look at the word signalling. A muscle can pull on a bone after a message arrives. The question wants ways to send the messages in the first place. One uses nerve cells. The other sends chemical signals through the blood.

clips.stepText: A quick movement alone does not tell you which centre controls it. Picture catching a ball without losing your balance. That takes timing. A hand that pulls away from heat illustrates the short protective circuit asked about in a different question.

clips.stepText: After rain, look at a school garden. Plants, insects, wet soil and air all matter. The living things and their surroundings make one system.
clips.mathToSpeechText: After rain, look at a school garden. Plants, insects, wet soil and air all matter. The living things and their surroundings make one system.
clips.spokenLine: After rain, look at a school garden. Plants, insects, wet soil and air all matter. The living things and their surroundings make one system.

clips.stepText: Knowing which creatures you saw is only part of the picture. In a school garden, insects and plants interact with soil, rain and light. Include the living groups and their surroundings if you want to describe the whole system.

clips.stepText: Start with food because that tells you which way to draw the arrow. Think of a grasshopper chewing grass. The insect gets some of the energy the grass stored. The arrow goes towards the insect because it receives that energy.

clips.stepText: A predator cannot get all the energy its prey once ate. Think of a grasshopper jumping before a bird catches it. The grasshopper has already used some of its food to move. Some of that energy has been released as heat.

clips.stepText: Carbon keeps changing where it is stored. Picture a growing bean plant. It takes carbon from the air while it makes food. When organisms break down some of that food, carbon can move back into the air as a gas.

clips.stepText: Plants need nitrogen to build useful molecules, yet the gas in the air is hard for most organisms to use. Think of a bean root with nodules. Some bacteria there turn the gas into a form that can enter living matter.

clips.stepText: A puddle can disappear without a person taking any water away. The water enters the air as vapour. If moist air cools, drops can form. Follow where the water goes rather than thinking that the puddle’s water has been destroyed.

clips.stepText: When a question says something moves, ask whether it is energy or material. You can trace a carbon atom into a leaf and back to the air. Energy used in that leaf can leave as heat. Keep those journeys separate.

clips.stepText: Imagine picking one bean from each of two bowls. The two picks make a pair. A young plant gets one version of a gene from each parent.

clips.stepText: What you see cannot always tell you both gene versions. Think of Mendel’s round peas. A round seed can have two copies of the round version or only one. The seed shape looks alike even though the pairs differ.
clips.mathToSpeechText: What you see cannot always tell you both gene versions. Think of Mendel’s round peas. A round seed can have two copies of the round version or only one. The seed shape looks alike even though the pairs differ.

clips.stepText: Every new pair needs one contribution from each parent. Picture a pea plant with two versions of the gene for seed shape. Each egg or pollen cell gets just one version. That separation is why a cross has different possible outcomes.

clips.stepText: Separate two traits in your mind before combining them. Mendel considered pea seed colour and shape together. For unlinked genes, a gamete’s version for colour need not tell you its version for shape. A one-trait question needs only one pair.

clips.stepText: Why count two mixed pairs? They come from different contributions, even though they look the same. Start with what each parent can pass on. Pair the choices one at a time. Only then count the seed shapes. The order keeps the two ratios apart.

clips.stepText: Start with the surprising seeds in the question. Two yellow parents can produce a white outcome. Both must be able to pass on the version whose effect is hidden in them. Then check that the ratio fits this explanation.

clips.stepText: The strongest clue is the pair of parents, not just the number of yellow seeds. Both parents look yellow but can pass on a version for white. Work from that clue before assigning the capital letter in the cross.
